author: Beth Copenhaver
title: The Virginia Comfort Food Locals Can't Stop Arguing About - NewsBreak
text:
By Beth Copenhaver ,
7 hours ago
Comfort foods bring joy, nourishment, and, almost always, a spirited debate. That’s certainly true of the top comfort food in Virginia: the ham biscuit. Now, you may be wondering how such an elegantly simple, time-tested handheld can cause conflict. The answer depends on what kind of ham is used, and while city ham versus country ham may not sound like much of a controversy, let’s just say people have their opinions.
What Is the Ham Biscuit, Virginia’s Most Argued-Over Comfort Food? Photo by L. Allen Brewer via Flickr Creative Commons In case you’ve yet to try it, a ham biscuit is pretty straightforward—a biscuit or roll filled with sliced ham. But the fact that the recipe is so simple is the very reason it’s so debated. For instance, should the biscuit be a true biscuit , buttery and flaky, or a simple dinner roll? Should it be served warm or room-temperature? Perhaps a bit of butter or mustard to the side? But none of these questions gets to the heart of the argument: which kind of ham should be used in a true Virginia ham biscuit?
This is what brings us to the country-versus-city debate. Country ham is typically cured and salty, sometimes smoked, giving the dish a certain sturdiness. On the other hand, city ham (like you’d order from a deli) is sliced thin, softer, and overall milder in flavor. As you’ve probably already guessed, there isn’t any “right” answer here, and every iteration of the ham biscuit has its place in Virginia’s culinary identity . Even so, let’s dive into the history and how this argument got started in the first place.
Why Virginia Locals Can’t Agree on the Best Ham Biscuit Photo by Tom Ipri via Flickr Creative Commons I have a hunch that the reason locals can’t agree on one best kind of ham biscuit is that they’re all good. Naturally, certain regions of the state have developed a preference, and this is probably regional. The Tidewater region, Southwest region, Appalachia, Shenandoah Valley, Richmond area, NoVa, and Central Virginia all have their unique food identities, and ham biscuits belong to all of them.
The history of the ham biscuit in Virginia most likely began near the coast, where mild and humid winters allowed for hams to be aged for up to 18 months without ever needing to be frozen. This traditional method of preserving—using salt and smoke—is also what gives Virginia ham its distinct flavor when compared to brined hams. (Queen Victoria reportedly preferred Virginia hams over European-cured hams.) Of course, with the development of commercial refrigeration after World War II, milder ham became more widely available. Today, you’ll find both, with variations as unique as the towns that serve them.
Where To Try Ham Biscuits in Virginia: Both Sides of the Deba te Photo by MAX + CO PHOTO – stock.adobe.com So where do you fall on the debate of country ham versus city ham? If you need to do a little more research, here are a few places where you can try excellent ham biscuits in Virginia:
The Virginia Diner (Wakefield) — A longtime staple serving iconic Virginia dishes, including country ham biscuits Exchange Cafe (Barboursville) — A cozy restaurant outside of Charlottesville with a locally loved cheddar chive biscuit and applewood smoked ham The Smithfield Inn (Smithfield) — Perhaps the single best place to go in Virginia for country-style Virginia ham biscuits So, as you can see, there’s really no way to declare a clear winner. Country ham may be the traditional favorite, but city ham has certainly given the ham biscuit a versatile (and delicious!) identity. Looking for even more comfort food in Virginia? Check out Mama J’s , a legendary restaurant in Richmond.
